name: fasting

attributes.attribute: Celtic ritual, troscad in Irish and ymprydio in Welsh
tradition of protest in Ireland and Wales
only reprisal for a harmed person
honour price kings and bards could dodge

sources: Kelly, Fergus. A Guide to Early Irish Law. Vol. III. Dublin: School of Celtic Studies, Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, Early Irish Law Series, 1988, 182+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fasting was a Celtic ritual with real force. In Irish it took the name troscad, and in Welsh ymprydio. To fast against an enemy stood as a tradition of protest in Ireland and Wales. Old Irish narrative uses ritual fasting, or the hunger strike, as a frequent device. Those stories mirror early Irish custom. Under the Brehon Laws, ritual fasting held standing as an established way to compel justice and to establish individual rights. Tradition calls it an infallible way to open the gates of a great warrior fortress. A victim of a wrong sat on the doorstep of the wrongdoer. He took no food and told passersby of the crime. Even persons of lower rank could press for redress this way. They sat at the door of the person accused and refused food until justice was paid. Kings and bards could dodge the eric, or honour price. For the harmed person, fasting stood as the only reprisal. The protest often worked and set matters right. Christian saints, so tradition says, fasted at the grave of Fergus mac Róich. He rose from death and then recited the Táin for them. The practice is not uniquely Celtic. Hindu tradition knows the same rite as dharnia. It returned time and again as nonviolent protest. Irish political life saw it recur through the 19th and 20th centuries.

okr.objective: Fasting, the Old Irish troscad, compels justice as a ritual protest.
key_results: The Brehon Laws treat ritual fasting as an established way to compel justice.
Tradition credits it with opening the gates of a great warrior's fortress.
Saints fasted at the grave of Fergus mac Róich before he rose and recited the Táin.
Hindu dharnia parallels it, and Irish politics revived the rite across two centuries.
